title: Way Seeking Mind
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of being present in the moment, free from distractions and preconceptions. By cultivating mindfulness and trust in the process, we can find gratitude and purpose in our daily lives, even in the face of challenges and setbacks. This approach is rooted in Heigaku Talus Latona's personal journey, which was shaped by their experiences as a caregiver, martial artist, and explorer of Eastern spiritual traditions, ultimately leading them to prioritize relationships, well-being, and personal growth.

sentences.text: There is the uncreated, and there appears to be an individual named Talus.
There is a mission to examine how the way of being and the individual mind touch each other.
This mission to trace the circumstances and causes leading to now is titled the way seeking mind.
A shuso's way seeking mind talk is usually a story beginning with their birth.
In this case, let's start with the present and explore how it came about.
This is Red Cedar Zen Community.
If you're looking for the Christian dharma talk, you're in the wrong, sorry, the Christian concert, you're in the wrong classroom.
You want the one next door up there.
I have been invited to be the head student for a few weeks.
I have been practicing Zen for almost ten years and some form of sitting meditation for almost twenty.
The most proximate aspect of the present outside of Zazen is my relationship with my wife Diane.
I am grateful to her on literally a daily basis, and grateful to have her in my life.
Together we operate Joy Heart Farm, a few acres of pasture and some garden.
While we both work on all aspects of the property, the house pets, rabbits, chickens and yaks are managed by her, while I manage the vegetables, trees, bees and mechanical infrastructure.
One of the creatures living in our home often causes the biggest messes that she has to deal with.
That would be me.
Did you know that a kitchen stove makes an excellent soldering bench?
It's a fireproof work surface, and it's got these preheating elements you can use, and even an exhaust fan for the fumes.
While Diane follows a different spiritual path than I do, it is a complimentary path, that's complimentary with an E, and I couldn't be sharing today with you without her support.
I also love my job as a hospital engineer lead in the plant operations and maintenance department of Peace Health St.
Joseph Medical Center.

I lead a crew of seven guys who perform maintenance and repairs on the boilers, generators, pumps, heat exchangers, fans, motors, valves and other machinery that provide heating, cooling, ventilation, medical gases, hot water, electricity and sewage service to the hospital.
While I have more desk work now than I used to, there is still plenty of excitement.
"I'm not sure if that pump impeller is stuck or if the shaft is broken, and it's too dark down there in the waste water pit to see anything."
"Yes, and the hatch is only 17 inches wide, there's no access."
"Hey, I bet we can fit Talus down there.
Hey Talus, put this harness on.
Double check that knot.
Okay, you ready?"
I wish everyone could love their job.
Working for a non-profit organization where the bottom line is about caring for people feels like right livelihood.

The lofty goals of caring and being patient centered wouldn't mean much without the continuous love that my team shows for each other as we work behind the walls every day, and that's no accidental circumstance, which I'll get to a bit later.
That's a broad view of the scope of this life at present.
Looking back a little ways on the path, I served as Eno, the Zendo coordinator, here for several years.

I've spoken before about how this position, like the doan and time keeper, offers the opportunity to really study the transition between formal seated meditation and the meditation of everyday life that involves making decisions and communicating with people.
Back and forth, back and forth.
Announce a form, return to seated meditation.
The mind is wandering, let it go.
Now, what is present?
Well, the intention in Zen, our intention may be to be present.
Maybe the practice of Zazen is more about returning to the present, the process of returning.
So instead of disappointment arising when we realize that we've been wandering in our minds, there's an opportunity for gratefulness to be arising.
Thankfulness that we can return.
Here's another chance to return.
Here's the tenth one in eight seconds.
I get to return.

As Eno I've experienced terror the first few times that the Dharma talk goes 25 minutes beyond the schedule, or word comes from the cooks that lunch is going to be late, and there is a room full of people looking on who've just received the signal that there is about to be an announcement about what's happening next.
Eventually I've learned to trust that it will all work out.
Similarly, I remember being disarmed by Norman's calm the first few times we rehearse a brand new ceremony 45 minutes before it's about to start.
True panicking wouldn't help, but it does always work out.
I used to say, everything works out.
You may be dead, but it will work out.
Now that's facetious, but there's a truth there: the idea that it could not work out is dependent on our deluded judgment and our misperceptions about the way the world is.
Community meditation practice usually works out well.
Ceremonies and our work together just kind of click.
There is one exception to Eno service working out well in the short term that has a strong influence on my choices for this practice period.
This event is still working out.
Of course they all are.
That's the nature of causation.
Last year at Samish we had a ceremony to present the names of the women ancestors to people who had undertaken the commitment to the ethical precepts formalized with Jukai.
That's symbolized by the blue rakusu.
Due to miscommunications or other errors, that ceremony didn't play out as planned.
I lapsed in attentiveness and effort on a number of factors.
An alignment of conditions magnified that disjointedness.
For example, more experienced doanryo chant leaders and bell ringers would probably have been able to respond more smoothly to unexpected events.
But all of the more experienced candidates were recipients in the ceremony, so they were unavailable.
In the end I observed, based on my three years of experience as being Eno, for ceremonies that went badly.
And badly was not without impact.
The ceremony was supposed to be a long overdue recognition and celebration of the impact that our women ancestors have had on our practice.
The patheticness of the ceremony ended up offending some of the people that it should have been honoring.
This ceremony honoring women leaders was planned out and implemented by three men.
Exclusively.
Guiding teacher Norman Fischer, spiritual director Tim, and myself as Eno.
The irony isn't lost on me that I am a man consciously stepping into the role of head student, complaining that our community has still plenty of work to do following more female leadership.
I do recognize that we men are the ones who have to change.
Now we all, everyone, have to take responsibility for finding our blind spots and learning what's in them.
And I thank the women who have had the courage to point that out to me.
Hey, blind spots and courage, wouldn't that make some excellent topics for a study group?
So we'll be doing that soon.

Zenshin, Florence Caplow, and Reigetsu Susan Moon have offered a pre-release copy of the Record of the Hidden Lamp, koans and stories from 25 centuries of awakened women, scheduled to be published sometime this year.
Holding the manuscript for the Record of the Hidden Lamp, I feel as honored as though I were holding an original parchment of the Blue Cliff Record, freshly penned by Yuanwu Keqin.
We are grateful to Florence and Susan for offering these overlooked treasures to the world and for allowing their study during this practice period.
Saturday and Monday classes.
Let's continue our trip back in time and note some other impactful experiences I've had in Zen.
In January 2010 I had the opportunity to participate in a three week session of residential practice at Green Gulch Monastery.

Besides opening to clarity, being exposed to the teachings on caring for karmic beings by Tenshin Reb Anderson, I found residential practice to be a way of right living that provides awakening and environment to flourish.
My life will include more residential practice in the future.
In 2008 I undertook a formal vow to uphold the 16 precepts in the Jukai ceremony.
I undertook this vow again when Diane and I were married on Mount Baker by Tim.
Over the course of the years of practice, Norman and Tim have gifted me by applying just the right balance of encouragement and guidance.

In the year of study and preparation for the Jukai ceremony, Lee Lordot and I met regularly to share and reflect on our journey into what it would mean to live acutely aware of how our actions impact others.
Lee has been a faithful sounding board and true Dharma friend since we met on a mountains and rivers retreat.

Just as sitting together with [unclear: "dulled collars"] in a silent Dharma hall provides a container conducive to being more aware of our oneness with the world, I find that the sacred purity exposed in an alpine forest or boulder field provides a similar opportunity.
So how did Zen find me?
My profound meditation for many years was the practice of martial arts.

When the opportunity arose to expand sitting meditation from a private endeavor and become a member of a community, I was at the time living on a very cramped sailboat in Drayton Harbor, averaging two to three hours a day of shuai jiao kung fu and tai chi chuan practice.
I would get up at four o'clock in the morning, go lock myself in the marina's public restroom, and practice for an hour before getting ready for work.
I had started with martial arts in seventh grade.
The shuai jiao I was practicing is a throwing art, a precursor to Aikido or Judo.
I was aware of the strong spiritual component to kung fu.
After all, it is reputed to have originated at Shaolin Temple under Bodhidharma.
However, I didn't understand at the time the spiritual aspect to the way of life – that's the way of life in capital letters – that my shuai jiao kung fu teacher was presenting.
So I sought out the closest available spiritual teachings to the Chan Buddhism and Taoism that kung fu evolved in, their descendant known as Soto Zen.
Looking at the pillars of my life that I presented earlier – martial arts, my wife, home life, my job, and Zen – it wasn't possible to engage in all of them with the quality time they deserved.
So after a difficult process of introspection about priorities, I let go of martial arts.
I had been married previously.
I will use the name Tasha.
We met at the University of Colorado, married, and moved to Northern California.
Over a few years, personality quirks that made Tasha endearing grew stronger into disabilities and then into incapacitating mental illness.
Tasha is schizophrenic.

For a while we adjusted, working together to counteract the voices in her head, abandoning rental agreements on a regular basis, and quitting jobs, as she fled from one town to another, eventually landing in Bellingham.
In San Francisco, we were homeless for a few months, living out of our car.
Eventually conversation became no longer possible, and I spent a few years in the role of caregiver, but without the legal authority to override her most misguided decisions.
During this difficult time, I was unable to practice martial arts or even maintain friendships, and was living with the one I loved who was absent.
Occasionally she was willing to venture out, and we both found some comfort meditating at the Santa Cruz Zen Center.
I was defeated by the challenge of being a caregiver without also being an enabler to an unhealthy lifestyle outside of institutionalization.
When her illness became severe enough that I felt her to be a danger to herself, to me, and to others, I heeded the advice of friends and family and initiated separation.

Turning to a very different aspect of life to explore how I came to my present job, as I was leaving Peace Corps, I faithfully performed all of the What Color Is Your Parachute career decision activities.
What coalesced strongest were two points.
One, that I enjoyed and excelled at working with the relationships between mechanisms, and two, that I wanted to work in the blue collar sector.
To study mechanisms, I got a degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Colorado, and to apply it to skilled manual labor, I worked in facilities maintenance.
One spiritual guide at this time was my supervisor at Applied Materials, where microchips are made.

Microchip making is a nasty affair involving lots of sulfuric acid; hydrofluoric acid, which causes mild burns to skin as it passes through, seeking the calcium in bones; and silane, which burns fiercely if it comes into contact with air.
Ray had worked in the industry for years, had seen it all, and Ray knew the difference between a real safety hazard and a fruitless panic about some more equipment about to eat itself up.

In response to a common situation such as, "Ray, the chlorine pumps have burned out and now the acid pit is about to overflow into the copper pad and destroy the neutralizer," he taught me the mantra: "Alright, I'll be right there."
This was usually followed by the words, "Just let me finish my cigarette."
When I started working at St.
Joseph Hospital, I dropped into a hornet's nest of warring factions.
The department management was being slowly pushed out by the administration, and the departing management responded by steering the department into being even more deeply mired.
I managed to support and gain the respect of both the outgoing managers as well as the new director brought in to clean things up.
When a new lead engineer position was posted, I thought myself to be a good candidate, but the notion of supervising the former lead engineer felt wrong.
I convinced the new director that two team leader positions were needed.
He said, "Write out exactly how this would work."
Thus I wrote my own job description.
The former lead engineer and I were hired as team leaders.
When the two of us were asked to join the director in hiring a manager to replace the departing managers, we hired one of my supervisees to be our boss.
The three of us have been working closely for seven years now.
Of course, there is the occasional disagreement between us, but discussions are never anything but calm, genuine exploration of others' perspectives.
Employee satisfaction scores in the department have gone from 40% to 85%, and productivity has been rising continuously.
That's a technical way of saying that people care about each other, about our patients, and about the work that we do.
This drastic change would not have been possible without Buddha-inspired values and reflections.
As I said, I studied engineering after completing my Peace Corps assignment.
As a volunteer in an arid deforested region of Uganda in East Africa, my official assignment was community forestry, teaching people to cultivate trees to combat erosion.

However, in studying how I could have the greatest positive impact on people's lives, I determined that it included connecting people with information and other resources wherever they identified the need, such as business skills, fuel conserving stove technology, bread making, fruit drying, and beekeeping.
In early December of my first year there, my father informed me that he was going to have a growth removed from one of his lungs.
A few weeks later I received news that the surgery was successful.
A teacher friend of mine invited me to spend Christmas at his home village.
So on Christmas Eve we left the village where I was living, took a shared Matatu taxi 80 miles to the county seat to catch another minibus where we would head off on another side road to his home.

While we were getting gas, I saw a Peace Corps vehicle from the capital parked across the street in this remote town, and I said to my friend, "I don't think I'm going to be able to spend Christmas with you."
Flying home on Christmas Day to my father's funeral, passenger traffic was ironically light, given just how crazy it is the rest of the season.
I was reading a book I had gotten from the Peace Corps library, an introduction to meditation by Ram Das.
The hardest part about being home was the pain that my mother and brother were experiencing.
I felt sad but peaceful about Dad's death.
We had parted on good terms, and at the same time it was blissful to see my girlfriend again.
We promised to become engaged upon my return to the U.S.
A few months later, back in Uganda, the demise of that relationship was the most excruciating period of my life.
On Saturday mornings I would get up before sunrise and ride my bicycle 20 miles to the next town where there was a telephone.
There I would wait for a call at the agreed upon time.
Her frequent letters became scarce and several weekly phone calls were missed, belying the passion and profession of love when we did communicate.
During the six weeks of this hell, before I received a clear "it's over" through a third party, I sought solace in a rigorous daily meditation practice which I continued through my years in Africa.
This included an hour of sitting and Tai Chi every morning, with a two hour straight sit on Sundays.
Meditation then was an effort to escape from life.
A local merchant taught me the futility of that.
I had gotten lost in a large outdoor local market and I was wandering the aisles of dried fish, carved furniture and Swahili blankets spread out on mats.
She watched me and called out, "Hey, white man, what are you looking for?"
"I'm looking for the exit," I said.
"Oh," she responded, "we don't have that here."
The following Christmas my mother, brother and future stepfather came to visit.
I was counseled to call the man with my mother Shwento, meaning paternal uncle, because in Uganda it is customary for a widow to become the second wife to her brother in law.
Nwajira was a neighborhood boy hired by my Ugandan counterpart to help with the chores in our house.
I often helped Nwajira with his homework and generally looked out for him since he didn't get much attention as the seventh child of the second wife at home.
Nwajira begged me to take him to the capital city to greet my family and I agreed.
The motel room we stayed in, run by a convent, was rudimentary.
Two wooden slat beds with foam mattresses, a bench with a plastic basin, and a bare light bulb hanging in the center of the room.
We were there a day early and I sat on my bed reading while he lay staring up at the ceiling.

Suddenly he sat up and exclaimed, "I am going to finish school and work hard and someday I'll be able to build a house, and in my house I'm going to put a glass ball on the ceiling that produces light just like this one.
And am I even going to put a switch on the wall to be able to turn that light on and off just like this one?"
What does that teach us about our desires?
After the retreat you might want to ask me about Nwajira's first experience with indoor plumbing.
When my family departed, Schwento left me Jack Kornfield's book A Path with Heart, which I still recommend as a return to book on Buddhism.
In seventh grade a Peace Corps volunteer visited our social studies class and I decided at that time, at twelve years old, that this combination of adventure and service was the right path for me.
It is difficult to be accepted for Peace Corps service without a bachelor's degree, so after high school I earned a degree in natural resources management from Colorado State University.
My first exposure to Buddhism came in the form of Eastern philosophy courses, which I took as a part of my second major, philosophy.
Outside of the classroom my friends and I frequently stayed up well into the night, not drinking, but debating the foundations of knowledge or ethical relativism or whatever.
I enjoyed pulling evangelicals into debates and referencing scripture to counter their claims.
That includes both Christian evangelicals as well as Hare Krishna evangelicals.
In high school in Illinois I spent several summers working at Shady Oaks Camp for Children with Cerebral Palsy, developing their computer lab.
A number of the campers had muscle control only over their eyes and jaw.
Being told a story by someone who can only move their eyes is a humbling experience.
As is the elation of hooking up a sensor to the chin of someone who knows how to read, but can only make the sounds meaning four different things: yes, no, drink and bathroom.
And suddenly with the computer input they were able to select sequential letters on a monitor to spell out words.
I did not return to Shady Oaks the next summer, taking advantage instead of the opportunity to spend the season studying a cactus that lives in the tree canopy of the Costa Rican cloud forest.
I was an Eagle Scout, though I quit Boy Scouts abruptly when my best friend in scouting was kicked out for writing a letter to the editor of our local newspaper revealing that he was gay.
This friend led me to my obscure sense of humor and taught me compassion for all beings, including beings called meat.

One day as a teenager back home, while taking a shower and considering the suffering experienced by animals in our factory agriculture system, I concluded that the suffering of animals is no less important than the suffering of humans.
I went on from there to identify that no creature was greater than any other, and therefore if God did exist he wasn't anything special.
I got dressed and informed my parents that I was leaving the Catholic Church.
I then considered myself a Unitarian Universalist.
I went on to become vegetarian for 10 years and strictly vegan for 10 years after that.
I am now mostly vegetarian.
You can read what that means by visiting www.mostlyvegetarian.com.
As my grandmother used to say, "Dot com, dot com, everything is dot com.
What the hell is dot com?"
I had been raised in a liberal Catholic family attending the student-oriented Newman centers.
As I grew up my father was a student financial aid administrator.

My mother was a substitute elementary school art teacher who later, at 40 years old, decided on a change of profession, got her PhD in psychology, and as of January 1st this year is retired from a full career as a therapist.
Excuse me, I seem to have just dislocated my Adam's apple.
I don't think that'll help, thank you.
See if I can stick it out.
My father's mother sang on the radio and wrote the pithy or shallow sayings in Hallmark greeting cards.
Her husband was a plumber and her father was a coal miner.
My mother's mother was mostly a homemaker.
Her husband insulated Pullman railroad cars and after World War II became a stock clerk for Bell Telephone.
Their parents were farmers, and though none of them passed seventh grade, their insights during debates I would have with them about human nature are some of the strongest that I have seen.
It is through the love and patience of my parents that I largely overcame being a mean thieving bully as a child.
Through my parents I developed my love of nature, having gone on my first tent camping trip at three weeks old.
My childhood was spent living in a village of population 200 in upstate New York, exploring the creek, fields and forests that surrounded our neighborhood.
Before that I was a single mother farming beans and barley in the Tungurupura province of Ecuador, but that's another story.
